# The EU AI Act for Commercial Teams: What Applies and When

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-eu-ai-act-for-commercial-teams/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: For a sales, marketing or customer team, the EU AI Act mostly applies through four routes: a short list of banned practices, a duty to support AI literacy, transparency rules for chatbots, deepfakes and AI-written public-interest text, and stricter rules if a tool falls into a high-risk category such as recruitment or credit scoring. Most commercial teams are deployers of other firms' tools, not providers. After the Digital Omnibus, Annex III high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## Key points

- Prohibited practices have applied since 2 February 2025, and the Digital Omnibus adds bans on AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material from 2 December 2026.
- Article 4, as amended by the Omnibus, requires providers and deployers to "support the development of AI literacy" of staff, without guaranteeing a set level for any individual.
- Article 50 transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026, with a grace period to 2 December 2026 for marking output from generative systems already on the market.
- Annex III high-risk obligations, which include recruitment, credit scoring and life and health insurance pricing, apply from 2 December 2027; Annex I product-embedded systems from 2 August 2028.
- Fines for most operator and transparency breaches reach EUR 15 million or 3% of worldwide turnover; for SMEs the lower of the two applies.

## Provider or deployer: which one is your team

The Act assigns duties by role. A provider develops an AI system or places it on the market under its own name. A deployer uses a system under its own authority in a professional setting. A marketing team using a copywriting tool, a sales team using a CRM assistant and a service team using a vendor's chatbot are deployers.

The line moves when a team builds. A company that wires a model API into its own branded website assistant may be the provider of that assistant, and takes on the provider duties that come with it.

## What applies to commercial teams, and when

| Date | What applies | Commercial relevance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 February 2025 | Prohibited practices (Article 5) and AI literacy (Article 4) | Bans include manipulative techniques causing significant harm and emotion inference in the workplace |
| 2 August 2025 | General-purpose AI model rules and penalties | Mainly falls on model providers, not on their business customers |
| 27 July 2026 | Digital Omnibus amendments in force | Literacy duty softened to "support"; high-risk dates moved |
| 2 August 2026 | Article 50 transparency duties | Chatbot disclosure, deepfake labels, AI-generated public-interest text |
| 2 December 2026 | New Omnibus prohibitions; end of Article 50(2) grace period | Generative tools must mark synthetic output in machine-readable form |
| 2 December 2027 | Annex III high-risk obligations | Recruitment, credit scoring, life and health insurance pricing |
| 2 August 2028 | Annex I high-risk obligations | AI embedded in regulated products such as machinery |

**Transparency.** Article 50(1) requires providers of systems that interact directly with people to tell those people they are dealing with an AI, unless that is obvious. A website sales assistant or a voice agent qualifies. Article 50(2) requires providers of generative systems to mark output as artificially generated in a machine-readable format. Article 50(4) puts two duties on deployers: disclose deepfake images, audio and video, and disclose AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. The text duty does not apply where a person has reviewed the content and someone holds editorial responsibility for it.

**Prohibited practices.** Two are worth checking: manipulative or deceptive techniques that materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm, and inferring emotions in the workplace, which can catch call-coaching tools that score sellers' emotional state.

**High-risk uses.** Annex III lists eight areas. The ones a commercial function is most likely to touch are recruitment and worker management, creditworthiness of individuals, and risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance. Scoring business accounts for sales priority is not on the list. A deployer of a high-risk system must follow the provider's instructions, assign human oversight to competent people, keep logs for at least six months, inform workers before workplace use, and tell individuals when the system is used in decisions about them.

**Standards.** On 14 October 2026 the Commission published EN 18286, a quality management system standard prepared by CEN and CENELEC, as the first harmonised standard under the Act. Providers of high-risk systems that follow it gain a presumption of conformity for the requirements it covers, including the Article 17 quality management system. Its use is voluntary, and it is aimed at providers, so commercial teams acting as deployers will mostly meet it through their vendors.

> The Act asks most commercial teams for an inventory, a disclosure and a person who reviewed the output. Few need more before December 2027.

## A practical checklist

| Step | Question | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inventory | Which tools use AI, including features inside existing software? | List with owner and vendor |
| Role | For each, are we provider or deployer? | Role column, with built tools flagged |
| Transparency | Does it talk to customers, or generate images, audio, video or published text? | Disclosure wording and placement |
| Risk class | Does it touch hiring, consumer credit or life or health insurance? | High-risk flag and 2027 plan |
| Literacy | Have the people using it been trained on its limits? | Training record |
| Oversight | Who reviews output before it reaches a customer? | Named approver per use |

The last line is the **lowob** rule that nothing sends without a person. It is not required for every use, but it supports the editorial-responsibility exception for published text and the oversight duty for high-risk systems.

## lowob takeaways

- **Settle the role first.** Using a vendor tool makes you a deployer; building your own assistant may make you a provider.
- **Transparency is the near-term duty.** Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026 to chatbots, deepfakes and public-interest text.
- **High-risk is narrow for commercial teams.** Hiring, consumer credit and insurance pricing are the main triggers, from December 2027.
- **Review creates the exemption.** Human editorial control takes published text out of the disclosure duty.

## Common questions

### Does the EU AI Act apply to marketing teams?

Yes, mainly through AI literacy, the prohibitions and Article 50 transparency duties, such as labelling deepfakes. Most marketing uses are not high-risk.

### Do AI chatbots have to disclose that they are AI under the EU AI Act?

Yes. From 2 August 2026, providers must design systems that interact with people so those people are told they are dealing with an AI, unless it is obvious.

### When do the EU AI Act high-risk rules apply?

After the Digital Omnibus, Annex III high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027 and Annex I product-embedded obligations from 2 August 2028.

### Is AI lead scoring high-risk under the EU AI Act?

Scoring business accounts is not listed in Annex III. Credit scoring of individuals, recruitment and life or health insurance pricing are.
